query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A Ni-based superalloy (e.g., Inconel 718) subjected to uniaxial tensile tests from room temperature to about 700°C will exhibit stable or slightly increasing yield strength and ductility up to moderate temperatures due to precipitation strengthening and controlled dislocation motion, followed by a reduction in strength beyond approximately 650–700°C as precipitate coarsening accelerates.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, solution-treated Ni-based superalloy (e.g., Inconel 718) in its standard age-hardened condition.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of temperature (room temperature, 200°C, 400°C, 600°C, 700°C) during uniaxial tensile tests, with concurrent microstructural analysis to track precipitate size and distribution.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric environment; heating to target temperatures (200–700°C) with controlled strain rates for mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: γ′/γ″ precipitates in the Ni-based matrix that coarsen as temperature increases and influence dislocation dynamics.
generation.mechanism: Precipitate-induced strengthening inhibits dislocation motion at lower to moderate temperatures; at higher temperatures, precipitate coarsening and increased atomic diffusion ease dislocation activity, leading to reduced strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Initial maintenance or minor rise in yield strength and ductility, followed by a measureable drop in both as testing temperature surpasses ~650–700°C.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature yield strength and ductility of the solution-treated, aged Ni-based superalloy prior to elevated-temperature testing.
generation.boundary: Short-term tests of up to 1-hour dwell at each temperature step; behavior at temperatures above 700°C or longer exposure durations is beyond the scope of the initial study.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature at which the decline in strength and ductility initiates may vary depending on specific alloy composition and thermal history prior to testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce multiple batches of solution-treated Inconel 718, subject them to incremental tensile tests (25°C, 200°C, 400°C, 600°C, 700°C) at a constant strain rate, and conduct post-deformation microstructural examination.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at each temperature
Elongation to fracture at each temperature
Quantitative analysis of precipitate size distributions in tested specimens
Characterization of dislocation substructures via electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If yield strength does not remain stable or slightly increase up to ~600°C, or significant precipitate coarsening does not coincide with the onset of strength reduction above ~650–700°C, then the hypothesis is refuted.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates.
